planting.note: Grow as a cool, shaded houseplant or greenhouse specimen in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix with constant humidity; this Andean cloud-forest species blooms best when nights stay below 65°F.

directions: Masdevallia coccinea is a compact, tufted epiphyte from the high-elevation cloud forests of Peru and Bolivia, prized for its long-lasting, triangular flowers held on wiry stems well above the foliage. Flower color ranges widely across individual plants, from deep magenta and scarlet to soft pink, orange, and white, all with a glossy, almost lacquered sheen. Keep the roots constantly moist and the air cool and humid, since this species has no drought tolerance and declines quickly in heat above the mid-80s Fahrenheit. Divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain vigor and encourage new growths.
sources: American Orchid Society — Masdevallia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Masdevallia coccinea species profile
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Masdevallia collection notes

planting.note: Grow in a cool, shaded spot with a fine, open orchid mix and constant air movement; Masdevallia ignea comes from cool Colombian highlands and resents heat, so an air-conditioned room or shaded greenhouse suits it best.

directions: Masdevallia ignea is a Colombian cloud-forest species named for its intensely fiery orange-red to vermilion flowers, each borne singly on an upright stem above a low tuft of leathery leaves. It has long been used as a parent in breeding red- and orange-flowered masdevallia hybrids for its saturated, glowing color. The plant needs cool nights, high humidity, and steady moisture at the roots year-round, with no seasonal dry rest. Repot or divide only when the mix breaks down, since masdevallias resent excessive root disturbance.
sources: American Orchid Society — Masdevallia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Masdevallia ignea species profile
Ecuagenera — Masdevallia species reference

planting.note: Mount on a large slab or grow in a wide, shallow basket of coarse bark in bright, filtered light; Bulbophyllum echinolabium is a large warm-growing species that needs generous root space and steady warmth to bloom well.

directions: Bulbophyllum echinolabium is a warm-growing lowland species from Sulawesi, Indonesia, notable for producing one of the largest individual flowers in the genus, sometimes exceeding a foot across its extended sepals. The mottled maroon-and-yellow flower carries a hinged, bristled lip that rocks in the slightest breeze, an adaptation that helps attract the carrion flies that pollinate it, and the bloom emits a strong, unpleasant odor most growers keep away from living spaces when flowering. Water and fertilize generously through warm weather and provide bright, filtered light and free air movement around the large paddle-shaped leaves. Because flowers open singly and briefly, patient collectors value it more for novelty and scale than for a long floral display.
sources: American Orchid Society — Bulbophyllum culture notes
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Bulbophyllum echinolabium species profile
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Bulbophyllum collection reference

planting.note: Grow in a large basket or pot of chunky bark in bright, filtered light with heavy watering; Bulbophyllum phalaenopsis is among the largest-growing bulbophyllums and needs a big container and constant moisture to support its massive pleated leaves.

directions: Bulbophyllum phalaenopsis is a spectacular New Guinea highland species named for its huge, deeply pleated leaves, which can reach two feet in length and rival small Phalaenopsis plants in size. Flower spikes emerge from the base of each pseudobulb bearing several large, dusky maroon-and-cream striped blossoms with the same hinged, mobile lip characteristic of the genus. It is a heavy feeder and heavy drinker relative to most orchids, needing constant moisture, high humidity, and generous fertilizer during active growth to support its outsized foliage. Give it plenty of room, since crowded roots and cramped pots quickly stunt this naturally massive plant.
sources: American Orchid Society — Bulbophyllum culture notes
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Bulbophyllum phalaenopsis species profile
Andaman Orchids — Bulbophyllum species reference

planting.note: Grow in a well-draining bark mix in bright, filtered light with cool nights in fall to encourage flowering; Zygopetalum intermedium is a Brazilian species that tolerates temperatures similar to cattleyas.

directions: Zygopetalum intermedium is a Brazilian species valued for its intensely fragrant flowers, which combine olive-green sepals and petals heavily blotched in chocolate-maroon with a broad white lip streaked in violet-purple. Several blooms open together on an upright spike, filling a room with a sweet, spicy scent reminiscent of hyacinth. Keep the bark medium evenly moist through the growing season and provide cooler nights in autumn, which helps initiate the flower spikes. Divide overgrown clumps in spring once new growth resumes.
sources: American Orchid Society — Zygopetalum culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Zygopetalum intermedium species profile
Royal Horticultural Society — Zygopetalum cultivation

planting.note: Grow in a well-draining bark mix in bright, filtered light; Zygopetalum crinitum is a cooler-growing Brazilian species that appreciates slightly lower temperatures than other zygopetalums.

directions: Zygopetalum crinitum is a Brazilian species distinguished by the shaggy, deeply fringed crest on its white, purple-veined lip, a feature that gives the species its Latin name meaning "hairy" or "fringed." The sepals and petals are green to yellow-green, heavily marked with dark maroon-brown blotches, and the flowers carry a strong, sweet fragrance typical of the genus. It prefers slightly cooler conditions than many zygopetalums and benefits from a marked temperature drop at night during the cooler months to trigger bloom spikes. Water regularly during active growth and reduce slightly once flower spikes finish, since the plant has only a mild rest period.
sources: American Orchid Society — Zygopetalum culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Zygopetalum crinitum species profile
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Zygopetalum collection notes

common_name: Long-Tailed Spider Orchid (Costa Rican Spider Orchid)

planting.note: Grow in a medium pot or slatted basket with medium bark in bright indirect to partial direct light; Brassia longissima needs a large root run and generous light to bloom well.

directions: Brassia longissima is a Costa Rican and Panamanian species named for the extraordinary length of its narrow, tapering sepals, which can extend flowers to nearly a foot from tip to tip. The yellow-green flowers are heavily spotted with reddish-brown and have a light, pleasant fragrance, opening several per arching spike in spring. Like other spider orchids, the elongated, insect-leg-like segments mimic a female spider wasp, tricking male wasps into attempted mating and effecting pollination. Grow in intermediate temperatures with steady moisture and generous pot size, since a cramped root system limits flowering.
sources: American Orchid Society — Brassia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Brassia longissima species profile
Dodson, C.H. — Pollination biology of Brassia (Orchid Digest)

planting.note: Grow in a medium-to-large pot or basket with coarse bark in bright indirect light; Brassia 'Rex' is a vigorous primary hybrid that blooms reliably with less cultural fuss than many Brassia species.

directions: Brassia 'Rex' is a classic primary hybrid (Brassia gireoudiana × Brassia longissima) prized for producing some of the largest flowers in the genus, often spanning eight to ten inches across long, tapering, yellow-green sepals heavily spotted in brown. It is markedly more vigorous and floriferous than either parent species, making it a popular introduction to spider orchids for growers who want dramatic flowers without the pickiness of some species crosses. Provide bright light, a generous pot, and steady watering through the growing season to support its large pseudobulbs and broad leaves. Established plants can produce multiple flower spikes each spring, each carrying several long-lasting blooms.
sources: American Orchid Society — Brassia culture sheet
Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register — Brassia Rex registration
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Brassia collection notes

planting.note: Divide clumps in spring as new growth emerges and pot into a fine bark mix in bright, filtered light; Miltonia clowesii is a warm-growing Brazilian species tolerant of average home temperatures.

directions: Miltonia clowesii is a Brazilian epiphyte bearing star-shaped flowers with yellow-brown barred sepals and petals surrounding a crisp white lip marked with a bold purple-red blotch at the base. Several long-lasting flowers open on each upright spike in late summer and fall, held well above the flattened pseudobulbs and strap-like leaves. It grows well in typical warm room conditions and does not require the cooler nights that some Brazilian orchids demand. Keep the bark medium evenly moist during active growth and provide bright, filtered light for the best flower color.
sources: American Orchid Society — Miltonia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Miltonia clowesii species profile
Royal Horticultural Society — Miltonia cultivation

planting.note: Divide and mount or pot in a fine bark mix in bright, filtered light; Miltonia flavescens produces its best fragrance and flowering when given warm days and slightly cooler, humid nights.

directions: Miltonia flavescens is a Brazilian species bearing slender, star-shaped, pale yellow flowers with a lightly frilled white lip, held in graceful arching sprays well above the foliage. The blooms release a distinct sweet fragrance that intensifies in the evening, making it a favorite for growers who enjoy orchids near a porch or window at night. It tolerates slightly warmer conditions than many Miltonia relatives and adapts well to average home humidity if watered consistently. Repot or divide only when pseudobulbs outgrow the container, since the plant resents frequent root disturbance.
sources: American Orchid Society — Miltonia culture sheet
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Miltonia flavescens species profile
Marie Selby Botanical Gardens — Miltonia collection notes

planting.note: Grow in a shaded terrarium or houseplant setting in a peat- or coir-based terrestrial mix, never bark; Ludisia discolor 'Alba' lacks the coppery leaf veining of the species type, giving it a more subdued, uniformly green appearance prized by foliage collectors.

directions: Ludisia discolor 'Alba' is a cultivated color form of the popular jewel orchid that lacks the vivid rose-red venation of the typical form, instead showing plain, deep green, velvety leaves that some collectors prefer for a quieter, more understated look. Like the species, it is grown almost entirely for its creeping foliage rather than its small white flower spikes, which appear in late fall and winter but are secondary to the leaf display. It thrives in the same deep shade and warm, humid conditions as standard Ludisia discolor and grows in ordinary terrestrial potting mix rather than bark. Propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in moist mix, which is the standard way this form is maintained true to type.
sources: American Orchid Society — Ludisia discolor cultivation guide
Missouri Botanical Garden — Ludisia discolor plant finder
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Terrestrial orchids for indoor culture

planting.note: Grow in a shaded terrarium or houseplant setting in a peat- or coir-based terrestrial mix; 'Nigrescens' has the darkest, near-black leaf color of the commonly grown Ludisia discolor forms, showing its pink veining to dramatic effect.

directions: Ludisia discolor 'Nigrescens' is a richly colored form of the jewel orchid with leaves so deeply blackish-maroon they appear almost black in low light, crossed by a network of bright pink to coppery-red veins that stand out sharply against the dark background. It is grown for this striking foliage contrast rather than for its small white winter flower spikes, which are pleasant but incidental to the display. Culture matches standard Ludisia discolor: deep shade, warm temperatures, constant moisture in a terrestrial peat- or coir-based mix, and high humidity to keep leaf tips from browning. Propagate by rooting stem cuttings in moist mix, which reliably reproduces the dark coloring true to the parent plant.
sources: American Orchid Society — Ludisia discolor cultivation guide
Missouri Botanical Garden — Ludisia discolor plant finder
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Terrestrial orchids for indoor culture
